passages.t: Jehoshaphat seeks God, and sends teachers
passages.happening:
Jehoshaphat succeeds Asa and strengthens Judah against Israel (verses 1-2). ‘Now the LORD was with Jehoshaphat because he walked in the earlier ways of his father David. He did not seek out the Baals’ (verse 3), ‘but he sought the God of his father and walked by His commandments rather than the practices of Israel’ (verse 4). God establishes the kingdom in his hand, and he has riches and honor in abundance (verse 5). ‘And his heart took delight in the ways of the LORD; furthermore, he removed the high places and Asherah poles from Judah’ (verse 6).

In his third year he sends officials, Levites and priests through Judah. ‘They taught throughout Judah, taking with them the Book of the Law of the LORD. They went throughout the towns of Judah and taught the people’ (verse 9).
passages.hearers:
Asa's reign ended in decline. His son Jehoshaphat receives four chapters, more than any king of Judah between Solomon and Hezekiah, and his reign mixes deep faithfulness with a dangerous alliance with Ahab. This opening chapter is an unmixed picture of what the Chronicler thinks a good king does: he seeks God, removes idols, and puts God's word in the people's hands.

Jehoshaphat reigned twenty-five years, commonly dated about 872 to 848 BC, probably overlapping at first with his father's last years. He lived in the days of Ahab and Elijah. Kings gives him a brief, favorable summary; the teaching mission and the roster of troops are found only in Chronicles. Some Hebrew manuscripts and the Greek lack the name David in verse 3, making the comparison with Asa's own faithful early years. The Baals were local forms of the Canaanite storm and fertility god, whose worship Ahab and Jezebel were promoting in the north.

The Book of the Law was a scroll of Israel's law, most likely some form of the law of Moses, perhaps including Deuteronomy. When few could read and books were copied by hand, a traveling mission was how the law reached ordinary towns. Deuteronomy gave the Levites and priests the task of teaching, and here royal officials join them. To teach, lamad, is the root of the later word Talmud. Verse 6 uses a phrase that usually means pride, his heart was lifted up, in a good sense: his courage in the LORD's ways.
passages.later: The law said of God's words, ‘And you shall teach them diligently to your children and speak of them when you sit at home and when you walk along the road’ (Deuteronomy 6:7).
passages.asks: Jehoshaphat sent God's word to every town, carried by people who could teach it. Ask how God's word reaches you, and how it reaches the people near you. And ask what you could teach, simply, to someone who has never been taught.

passages.t: The dread of the LORD, and a strong kingdom
passages.happening: ‘And the dread of the LORD fell upon all the kingdoms of the lands that surrounded Judah, so that they did not make war against Jehoshaphat’ (verse 10). Philistines bring gifts and silver, and Arabs bring flocks of rams and goats (verse 11). Jehoshaphat grows greater and builds fortresses and store cities (verse 12). His commanders and their troops are listed, among them ‘Amasiah son of Zichri, the volunteer for the LORD’ (verse 16).
passages.hearers:
The chapter opens and closes with military strength, and between them stand Jehoshaphat's seeking of God and the teaching mission, with the dread of the LORD falling on the nations as the result. The structure puts the teaching of God's law at the center that holds everything else. The dread, pachad, is of the LORD, not of Jehoshaphat.

Tribute from Philistines and Arabs reflects the practice by which weaker neighbors sent gifts to a stronger king to keep peace; the Arabs were herders of the southern and eastern deserts, so their tribute came in flocks. The long list of names is typical of Chronicles and gave its readers real people and families behind the account. Amasiah is called the volunteer for the LORD, a phrase that recalls the willing gifts of 1 Chronicles 29. The troop numbers are the largest given to any king of Judah, and readers take them in the ways described for the numbers in chapter 13.
passages.later: David's leaders had given in the same spirit: ‘And the people rejoiced at the willing response of their leaders, for they had given to the LORD freely and wholeheartedly’ (1 Chronicles 29:9). Deborah's song begins, “When the princes take the lead in Israel, when the people volunteer” (Judges 5:2).
passages.asks: Among the commanders one man is remembered for having volunteered himself for the LORD. Ask what you would want to be remembered for in one line. And ask where you could give yourself willingly this year.
